summary: This proposed standard specifies a registration mechanism for the Host Identity Protocol, letting hosts register with services such as rendezvous servers or middleboxes. It obsoletes RFC 5203.

plainLanguage.summary: Before using a helper service, you sign up with it. This defines how a computer using HIP signs up with such helper services.

questions: how to register with a hip rendezvous server
how are hip registration lifetimes encoded
subtitle: How a Host Identity Protocol host signs up with a registrar for services such as rendezvous or middlebox traversal.

tldr.problem: Hosts using the Host Identity Protocol (HIP) need a generic way to register with a service, such as a rendezvous server or a middlebox, and to say how long the registration should last.
tldr.mechanism: A registrar announces its services in a REG_INFO parameter, a requester asks for them with REG_REQUEST, and the registrar answers with REG_RESPONSE or REG_FAILED. These ride on the HIP base exchange packets or on UPDATE packets, and lifetimes use a compact exponential encoding.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8003 obsoletes RFC 5203 and adds certificate-based authorization of requesters plus new failure types. It defines no specific services itself; other documents define registration types.

today: RFC 8003 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2016. It obsoletes RFC 5203, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Introduction and Terminology
sections.content:
RFC 8003 is an extension to the Host Identity Protocol (RFC 7401). It gives a host a generic way to register with a service. The service may be a HIP rendezvous server (RFC 8004) or a middlebox. The RFC makes no assumption about the type of service, and it does not say how to discover a service or how to interact with it after registration.

It defines these terms:

  • Requester: a HIP node asking a registrar for registration.
  • Registrar: a HIP node offering registration for one or more services.
  • Service: a facility giving requesters new capabilities at the HIP layer, such as firewalls that support HIP traversal or rendezvous servers.
  • Registration: shared state kept by a requester and a registrar. It has a finite lifetime and can be extended by re-registering.
  • Registration type: an 8-bit identifier for a given service.
sections.plainLanguage: A requester is the kid asking to join, a registrar is the person at the desk who signs kids up, and a service is the perk, like a locker. A registration is the sign-up slip that expires.

sections.title: How Registration Works
sections.content:
Registration reuses the HIP base exchange (the I1, R1, I2 and R2 packets of RFC 7401) or an existing HIP association. A host willing to act as a registrar SHOULD include a REG_INFO parameter in the R1 packets it sends to that requester. If it cannot currently provide services, it SHOULD send an empty REG_INFO and later announce available services in UPDATE packets.

To register, the requester puts a REG_REQUEST in an I2 or UPDATE packet. With no existing association, it SHOULD send the request as early as possible, in the I2. A registrar MAY end an association that carries no REG_REQUEST by including a NOTIFY of type REG_REQUIRED (error type 51) in the R2, and then no association is created.

On success the registrar replies with a REG_RESPONSE listing the granted types, plus zero or more REG_FAILED parameters for types it refused or could not provide. The reply is an R2 or an UPDATE, depending on whether the request came during the base exchange or on an existing association. Processing a REG_RESPONSE creates registration state at the requester, and processing a REG_REQUEST creates state at the registrar and possibly at the service.
sections.plainLanguage: When you come in to the club, the desk tells you which perks are on offer. You say which you want, and the desk gives you a slip for those it can give and a note about the ones it cannot.

sections.title: Authorizing Requesters
sections.content:
The registrar can identify the requester from the host identity in the I2. If it knows the Host Identities of all hosts allowed to register, it SHOULD reject unknown ones. Because preconfiguring them all may be infeasible, it SHOULD also support HIP certificates (RFC 8002).

A requester that has a suitable certificate SHOULD include it (or just the most suitable one) in a CERT parameter alongside the REG_REQUEST. If it has none, it SHOULD send the request without a CERT to see whether the registrar accepts it based on identity alone.

When a request arrives and the registrar requires authentication, it MUST first check whether the requester's HI is on the allowed list for every requested type. If so, it MUST proceed. If not, it looks for a CERT parameter. With none, it MUST reject with failure type 0 (additional credentials required). With a valid certificate issued for the requester and signed by a trusted issuer, it MUST proceed. Otherwise it MUST reject with the matching failure type, for example 4 (bad certificate), 5 (unsupported certificate), 6 (certificate expired), 7 (certificate other) or 8 (unknown CA).
sections.plainLanguage: If your name is not on the guest list, you can show a signed ID card. If you show none, the desk tells you to come back with one. If the card is torn, out of date or signed by someone nobody knows, the desk says which problem it was.

sections.title: The Four Registration Parameters
sections.content:
All four parameters use the HIPv2 TLV format of RFC 7401. Each carries a list of registration types and is protected by the HIP signature in the packet it rides in.

  • REG_INFO (type 930): sent by the registrar in R1, and in UPDATE when its offering changes. It holds a minimum and a maximum lifetime and the offered types. A requester SHOULD NOT ask for a lifetime outside that range.
  • REG_REQUEST (type 932): sent by the requester in I2 or UPDATE, with a requested lifetime and the preferred types in order of preference. A requester MUST NOT send more than one per packet, and MUST NOT ask for types the registrar has not offered. If the lifetime is out of range, the registrar SHOULD grant the minimum or maximum.
  • REG_RESPONSE (type 934): sent in R2 or UPDATE only when registration has succeeded, with the granted lifetime and types. The requester MUST be prepared for any lifetime, even one outside the announced range.
  • REG_FAILED (type 936): carries a failure type and the registration types that failed for that reason.

Failure type 2 (insufficient resources) means the requester MUST NOT retry at once and MAY try another registrar. Failure type 3 (invalid certificate) means it MUST NOT retry with the same certificate for the same services.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four kinds of notes: here is what we offer, here is what I want, here is what you got, and here is what you did not get and why.

sections.title: Lifetimes and Maintaining Registrations
sections.content:
Lifetimes are one octet in an exponential encoding. The value 0 means a lifetime of zero seconds and is used to request and grant cancellation. Any non-zero value is an exponent giving a lifetime of 2^((lifetime - 64)/8) seconds. That covers 255 durations from about 4 ms up to about 178 days.

Every requester and registrar MUST support a minimum lifetime of 10 seconds and SHOULD support a maximum of at least 120 seconds. These baselines were chosen to fit existing timeouts of state in middleboxes such as NATs and firewalls.

A requester MAY cancel early by sending a REG_REQUEST with zero lifetime, and the registrar SHOULD respond by granting a zero lifetime. A registrar, or an attached service, MAY cancel at its own discretion, but SHOULD then send a REG_RESPONSE with zero lifetime to all registered requesters. Registration type definitions MAY add their own parameter dependencies.
sections.plainLanguage: The membership slip has a countdown printed in a compact code. A zero on the slip means you are leaving or the club is ending your membership. Either side can end it early.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extension relies on the HIP base exchange and does not change its security properties, such as its digital signatures and HMAC. The RFC argues that the only new threat is the soft registration state created at the registrar.

Registrars act voluntarily and already accept being a Responder to potentially unknown hosts, so they store association state anyway. Adding some time-limited registration state should not introduce serious additional threats, especially since a registrar may cancel registrations at any time, for example because of resource constraints during an attack.
sections.plainLanguage: Signing people up means keeping a slip for each, but the slips expire and the desk can tear them up whenever it is too busy, so it is not much extra risk.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 5203
sections.content:
RFC 8003 obsoletes RFC 5203. The appendix lists three changes: references were updated to the revised HIP specifications, a failure type was added for insufficient resources at the registrar, and requester authorization based on certificates was added together with new failure types for invalid certificates.

IANA kept the parameter types 930, 932, 934 and 936, moved the references from RFC 5203 to this document, and added failure types 2 to 8 to the "Registration Failure Types" registry. The "Registration Types" registry defines no types, only 201-255 reserved for private use, and adding a type requires a new IETF specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The new rules add a way to prove who you are with an ID card, and more clear reasons for saying no.

messages.label: I2 (REG_REQUEST)
messages.note: Asks to register for a service.

items.label: Insufficient resources
items.desc: Do not retry immediately; may try another registrar.

items.label: Invalid certificate
items.desc: Do not retry with the same certificate for the same services.

items.label: Unsupported certificate
items.desc: The certificate is of an unsupported type.

items.label: Certificate expired
items.desc: The certificate is no longer valid.

items.label: Certificate other
items.desc: Could not be validated for some unspecified reason.

items.label: Unknown CA
items.desc: The issuing CA certificate could not be located or is not trusted.
